article.overview: An ultraviolet (UV) radiation detector is an instrument that records ultraviolet light arriving from a source. In a lunar context, the catalogue entry covers instruments that use ultraviolet light to observe the Moon's surface, its environment or distant targets. This article discusses two documented examples: the Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, which was placed on the lunar surface in April 1972 and is documented in the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report [3][6][7], and the Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), a far-ultraviolet instrument in lunar orbit [1][2][4][5]. The catalogue name is broad, so this article treats it as a class of instruments rather than one design.
article.description: Ultraviolet instruments on the Moon observe light outside the visible range. NASA describes LAMP as an instrument that maps the lunar surface in the far ultraviolet, searches for surface ice and frost in polar regions and images permanently shadowed regions illuminated only by starlight [1]. The LAMP help page calls it 'a small UV instrument' and a low-risk, high-heritage investigation based on a rebuild of an existing instrument [2]. The Apollo 16 camera recorded light 'in the invisible band of wavelengths between 50 and 160 nm' [3]. NASA describes it as the first Moon-based observatory, and the crew used it to photograph Earth in ultraviolet light [6]. The two examples differ in design, era and mission context, so their details should not be merged.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: For LAMP, the sources read identify three linked purposes: mapping the lunar surface at far-ultraviolet wavelengths, identifying exposed water-ice or frost in polar regions and imaging permanently shadowed regions lit only by starlight [1][2]. The LAMP help page also lists a demonstration of low-light vision for future landed missions among its objectives [2]. For the Apollo 16 camera, the NTRS record describes observations of Earth's atmosphere and geocorona, the solar wind and interplanetary hydrogen, and distant stars, nebulae and galaxies [3]. Because it was blind to visible light, it recorded few of the stars mapped by ground-based telescopes, mainly hot O, B and possibly A-class stars, with a limiting magnitude of at least 11 [3]. NASA's account emphasises the Earth observations. Carruthers described them as the first time the Earth had been photographed from a distance in ultraviolet light, showing the full extent of Earth's hydrogen atmosphere, polar auroras and the tropical airglow belt [6]. No source read reports a quantitative performance figure for either instrument, so this article makes no claim of achieved measurement beyond these qualitative results.
article.operating_principle: The sources read do not give a complete optical design for LAMP, and the primary design paper was not read in full. A secondary summary located in this run describes LAMP as a telescope plus Rowland-circle spectrograph, with an f/3 off-axis paraboloid primary mirror feeding a toroidal holographic grating, and a microchannel-plate detector with a solar-blind photocathode [8]. These design details were not confirmed on a primary page and must be checked against the Gladstone et al. paper [5] before reuse. For the Apollo 16 camera, the NTRS record gives an optical aperture of 7.5 cm [3]. The Smithsonian record describes an instrument that could work in spectroscopic and direct-view modes [7]. Its focal ratio, field of view and detector or film type are not stated in the records read.
article.scientific_importance: Permanently shadowed regions of the lunar poles are of scientific interest because they may hold water ice. The LAMP sources state that the instrument was designed to identify exposed water-ice deposits there and to image these regions using starlight [1][2]. LAMP is listed among the instruments of the LRO mission [4] and is documented in a dedicated instrument paper [5]. The Apollo 16 camera is significant as an early ultraviolet observatory on the lunar surface. NASA's 2020 article describes it as the first Moon-based observatory [6], and the NTRS record documents its Earth and stellar observations [3]. Its scientific results are described only qualitatively in the sources read, and no quantitative measurement is quoted here.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal set of physical specifications for an ultraviolet radiation detector. The two examples are different instruments from different eras. Mass and power values for LAMP appear only in secondary summaries located in this run; they are recorded as reported but unverified, and the numeric JSON fields are null. The Apollo 16 dimensions come from a museum's reconstructed backup model, not the flown unit.

examples.name: LRO Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP)
examples.type: Lunar orbital far-ultraviolet instrument on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.flight_status: Documented as an instrument on the LRO mission [1][2][4]. Current operating status was not confirmed in the sources read.

reported_unverified_values.source_notes: Mass 6.1 kg and minimum power requirement 4.5 W are attributed to the SwRI LAMP science page [8] as reported in a search summary; the page itself could not be fetched. Average power 4.0 W is attributed to Spaceflight Now [9] as reported in a search summary. The two power figures differ and are not verified on a primary page.

examples.design_heritage: LAMP is described as a rebuild of an existing instrument [2]. A secondary summary identifies the heritage as the ALICE family of ultraviolet spectrographs [8]; the Gladstone et al. paper, which would confirm this, was not read in full [5].
examples.notes: Numeric mass and power fields are null because the values were not confirmed on a primary page. No LAMP-specific dimensions or wavelength range were found in the sources read. Operational specifications are not stated in the sources read.

examples.name: Apollo 16 Far UV Camera/Spectrograph
examples.type: Historical lunar-surface ultraviolet camera and spectrograph (Apollo 16)
examples.flight_status: Documented as used on the Apollo 16 mission and set up on the lunar surface in April 1972 [3][6].
examples.design_heritage: Developed at the Naval Research Laboratory by George R. Carruthers, with Thornton Page credited as co-author of the Apollo 16 report chapter [3][6]. The Smithsonian describes the museum object as a reconstructed back-up engineering model (Serial Number 4) [7].
examples.notes: The 49.5 x 78.7 x 53.3 cm overall dimensions belong to the Smithsonian's reconstructed back-up model, which includes restoration work and replacement parts; they are not the flown unit's dimensions. The NTRS record gives the 7.5 cm aperture for the optical part. Mass, power, focal ratio, field of view, detector and film format are not stated in the records read. The chapter PDF was not retrieved.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not verified for the flown LAMP instrument. For the Apollo 16 camera, the Smithsonian lists an overall size of 49.5 x 78.7 x 53.3 cm for its reconstructed back-up engineering model (Serial Number 4) [7]. This is not a flight dimension.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: LAMP: a secondary summary reports about 6.1 kg [8], not verified on a primary page. Apollo 16 camera: not stated in the records read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LAMP: a secondary summary reports an average power of 4.0 W [9] and a minimum requirement of 4.5 W [8]. These figures differ and are unverified. Apollo 16 camera: not stated in the records read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The sources read do not give quantitative environmental requirements for either example. Qualitatively, LAMP is described as observing surfaces lit only by starlight in permanently shadowed regions [1][2], which is a low-light observing task. The Apollo 16 camera was placed in the Descartes highlands, in the shadow of the lunar module Orion [6], and was pointed at Earth on 21 April 1972 [3]. How either instrument handled lunar temperature, radiation, dust or contamination is not described in the sources read and is not assessed here.
article.limitations: The evidence base remains narrow. The primary LAMP design paper was identified but not read in full [5], and the Apollo 16 chapter body text was not retrieved [3]. No LAMP mass, power or dimension is verified from a primary page, and the Apollo 16 camera's flight mass and power are not stated in the sources read. Because the catalogue name is broad, these two examples may not represent every ultraviolet radiation detector.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The sources read describe LAMP as an instrument on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [1][4], which is a lunar orbiter. They do not describe how LAMP was integrated, launched or commissioned. The Apollo 16 camera was carried to the Moon on the Apollo 16 mission and placed on the surface by the crew [6]. The steps below separate what is documented from what is not.
transportation_process: LAMP integration, launch, cruise and lunar orbit insertion: not described in the sources read [1][4].
LAMP commissioning and operations: the LRO sources describe observation goals only [1][2]; interface details are not verified.
Apollo 16 camera transfer: the instrument travelled to the Moon on Apollo 16 and was placed on the surface by the crew [6]. The transfer method and stowage are not described in the sources read.
Apollo 16 camera setup: the crew set it up on the surface in the Descartes highlands, in the shadow of the lunar module Orion [6], and pointed it at Earth on 21 April 1972 [3].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 16 camera was placed on the surface by its crew [6]; the handling and setup method, including any mounting, is not described in the sources read. LAMP is an orbiter instrument [1][4], so surface deployment does not apply to it.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 16 mission is the historical surface example, documented in the 1972 Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report [3][6]. The LRO mission is the orbital example, with LAMP among its instruments [4]. NASA's 2020 article also lists later far-ultraviolet instruments that were not lunar payloads: an instrument with two far-UV cameras that flew on STS-39 in 1991, and the GIMI instrument launched on the ARGOS satellite in 1999 [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. LAMP is associated with LRO [1][4], and the Apollo 16 camera's mission context is documented in its report [3] and in NASA's article [6]. Compatibility for any future ultraviolet radiation detector would need its mass, dimensions, mounting, power, data and thermal interfaces checked against verified specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 camera is documented as an early ultraviolet observatory on the lunar surface. NASA describes it as the first Moon-based observatory developed by George Carruthers [6], and the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report chapter, published in 1972, records its use [3]. NASA's article also notes that Carruthers made the first detection of molecular hydrogen in space, using a sounding rocket, in 1970 [6]. LAMP is documented as part of the LRO mission [4] and in a dedicated instrument paper [5]; its operating history is not covered by the sources read.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: 1. Apollo 16 chapter: only the NTRS record and its descriptive text were read; the chapter body was not retrieved [3]. 2. LAMP design paper: Gladstone et al. was identified, but its full text was not read; the DOI page redirected to a publisher login, and the publication year is recorded inconsistently as 2009 or 2010 [5]. 3. LAMP mass (about 6.1 kg), average power (4.0 W) and minimum power requirement (4.5 W) are reported only in secondary summaries [8][9]; the SwRI page could not be fetched in this run, and the two power figures disagree. 4. No LAMP dimensions or wavelength range were found. 5. No flight mass, flight dimensions or power is verified for the Apollo 16 camera; the Smithsonian size applies to a reconstructed backup model [7]. 6. Only one image was verified from an official page [6]; Smithsonian object images were not verified, so none is included. 7. Current operating status for LAMP and for the Apollo 16 instrument was not confirmed. 8. No landing site or lunar location is recommended, as deferred by the user.

data_quality_notes: Rerun v2 of payload 130. The v1 files (ultraviolet_radiation_detector_payload_130.md, .json and .urls.txt) were not modified.
Web searches used in v2: 4. Page fetches attempted: about 12, of which several redirected, returned errors or were empty.

LAMP mass (about 6.1 kg), average power (4.0 W) and minimum power requirement (4.5 W) come from secondary search summaries [8][9]. They are recorded as reported text, not as numeric fields, because no primary page was fetched to confirm them. The two power figures disagree.
The SwRI LAMP science page (reference 8) could not be fetched in this run: the www host redirected and the www2 host returned a certificate error. Its content is taken from a search summary.
The Gladstone et al. LAMP paper was not read in full. The DOI 10.1007/s11214-009-9578-6 redirected to a publisher login. The DOI 10.1007/s11214-009-9662-9 returned 404 in v1 and is not used.

The one image (NASA, Carruthers and Conway with the Apollo 16 camera) has a direct JPEG URL that was retrieved; its embedded metadata matches the NASA caption, but pixel content was not visually confirmed.
A NASA shortlink (https://www.nasa.gov/?p=433412) was seen in an earlier search result. It contains a query string and was not used; the canonical image-article URL is cited instead.

Smithsonian object images: the record lists image identifiers NASM-A19830142000_PS01 to PS03, NASM-NASM2017-01977 and NASM-2006-23.06, but no direct image URLs were retrieved. No Smithsonian image is included.
The Apollo 16 chapter body text in the Preliminary Science Report was not retrieved; the NTRS record gives only a descriptive text and the 50 to 160 nm band.
The catalogue name 'Ultraviolet radiation detector' is generic. The two examples illustrate the class and do not define it.
All JSON URLs have had query strings and fragments removed.
